The best VAPT tool for a development team depends on what you need to prove. For a fast scanner in your pipeline,[OWASP ZAP](https://www.zaproxy.org/) and[StackHawk](https://codeant.ai/blogs/stackhawk-pricing) fit. For hands-on manual testing,[Burp Suite Professional](https://codeant.ai/blogs/burp-suite-pricing) is the standard toolkit. If you need each vulnerability proven with a working exploit, and a report you can hand to an auditor, a bank partner or an enterprise customer,[CodeAnt AI](https://codeant.ai/pentesting) runs AI-powered[black box](https://codeant.ai/pentesting/blackbox-pentesting) ,[grey box](https://codeant.ai/pentesting/graybox-pentesting) and[white box](https://codeant.ai/pentesting/whitebox-pentesting) pentests and delivers the report within 48 hours, then retests after every fix. It fits SaaS and fintech teams that ship every week and owe someone a pentest report.


CodeAnt AI has run 12,000 pentests and is trusted by more than 1,000 companies, including Fortune 500 companies like NRG, cybersecurity leaders like Commvault, and fast-growing companies like 11x and Sanas.


This guide compares seven tools developers use for VAPT in 2026, what each one proves, who has to run it, what it costs on the vendor's own page (checked November 6, 2026), and where scanning ends and a penetration test has to start.


## What Counts as a VAPT Tool for a Development Team?


[VAPT](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/what-is-vapt) stands for vulnerability assessment and penetration testing. The two halves answer different questions, and most tools only do one of them.


A vulnerability assessment asks what might be wrong. Scanners crawl your app, send known payloads and match versions against known CVEs. The[OWASP DevSecOps Guideline](https://owasp.github.io/www-project-devsecops-guideline/latest/02b-Dynamic-Application-Security-Testing) describes DAST as black box testing that finds weaknesses in a running application "by injecting malicious payloads", and notes these tools can run as part of a nightly scan with little interaction once configured.


A penetration test asks what an attacker can actually do. A tester, human or AI, chains findings together, logs in as different users, moves from one account to another or from a low-privilege role to admin, and shows the data that comes out. That is the part scanners cannot do on their own. The[OWASP Web Security Testing Guide](https://owasp.org/www-project-web-security-testing-guide/v42/4-Web_Application_Security_Testing/10-Business_Logic_Testing/00-Introduction_to_Business_Logic) says business logic flaws "cannot be detected by a vulnerability scanner" and that automating business logic abuse cases "is not possible" with those tools.


Why it matters to developers: the[OWASP Top 10:2025](https://owasp.org/Top10/2025/A01_2025-Broken_Access_Control/) keeps Broken Access Control at number 1 and reports that 100% of the applications tested had some form of it. Access control bugs sit behind the login, in the logic your team wrote, which is exactly where a scanner is weakest.


So a complete VAPT setup for a development team usually has two layers: a scanner in the pipeline for fast feedback on every build, and a penetration test that proves what is exploitable and produces the report your customers and auditors ask for.

## How Does Each Tool Fit a Developer's Workflow?


### CodeAnt AI: pentests that prove the exploit, tied to your code


CodeAnt AI starts from your attack surface, the domains, APIs and services an outsider can reach, then its agents chain what they find into attack paths and prove each one with a working exploit. Black box needs only your domain. Grey box adds test accounts, so the agents can try tenant, role and IDOR abuse. White box adds code access, so they can follow how a request reaches your data. Researchers confirm every critical finding before it reaches you. Findings go into Linear with the evidence attached, or you copy a ready prompt into your coding agent, and when you push a fix CodeAnt reruns the same attack to show it held. The same platform reviews pull requests on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Azure DevOps, so code findings and pentest findings live in one place.


Tradeoff: it is a scoped pentest, not a scanner you run on every commit. Pair it with a pipeline scanner, or with CodeAnt's own code review, for build-time feedback.


### Burp Suite: the manual tester's toolkit


Burp Suite Professional is the toolkit PortSwigger calls the world's number 1 for web penetration testing: an intercepting proxy and a set of tools for testing a web app by hand. PortSwigger also sells Burp Suite DAST for automated, CI-driven scanning and Burp AT, which it describes as agentic AI that extends human-led pentesting. Burp is excellent in skilled hands. The catch for a development team is that the tool does not do the test for you, so someone with the skills has to spend the time, and nobody outside your team signs the result.


See how it compares in[CodeAnt AI vs Burp Suite](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-burp-suite) .


### OWASP ZAP: the free scanner baseline


ZAP, now branded ZAP by Checkmarx and still an independent open-source project, describes itself as the world's most widely used web app scanner. Teams run it in CI or nightly to catch missing headers, injection points and known issues early. It costs nothing, but every false positive and every missed logic bug is your team's problem, and it does not produce a pentest report for an auditor or a customer's security team.


### StackHawk: testing inside the coding agent


StackHawk has moved closest to the developer. Wingman runs inside coding agents such as Claude Code, Cursor and Copilot, boots your app, probes it from an attacker's point of view and tells CI whether the commit is clean. It is a strong fit for teams writing a lot of AI-generated code. Its pricing page lists no pentest report, no human testing and no compliance mapping, so it complements a pentest rather than replacing one.


### Astra Security: scanner and pentest under one roof


Astra sells both halves of VAPT with public prices: DAST scanner plans, an autonomous Pentest Auto plan with a report for SOC 2, ISO 27001 and HIPAA, and a Pentest Expert plan with manual testing by certified experts. Retests are limited by tier, one human re-scan on Pentest Auto and two on Pentest Expert, which matters if you fix in several rounds.


### Intruder: same-day AI web app pentests


Intruder is known for continuous vulnerability scanning and attack surface monitoring. Its AI pentest covers web applications, connects to your repositories, delivers a report the same day with unlimited retests, and refunds the test in full if your auditor rejects the report. The AI pentest is web-app only, and the subscription plan prices are not shown on its pricing page.


See[CodeAnt AI vs Intruder](https://codeant.ai/blogs/codeant-ai-vs-intruder) for a side-by-side.


### Aikido: a pentest module inside a code security suite


Aikido bundles code scanning, cloud checks and an AI pentest. A typical pentest is $4,000 for one application and its main APIs, and Aikido does not charge when no high or critical issues are found. AutoFix can open a pull request from a finding. Aikido's own page says some standards and auditors still require a human-led pentest, which it offers on request.


See[Aikido vs CodeAnt AI](https://codeant.ai/comparison/aikido) .


## Is a Scanner in CI Enough, or Do You Still Need a Penetration Test?


For most teams that sell to businesses, no. Here is what we hear from engineering and security leads when they compare the two.


Scanners report what they recognise. One security lead who trialled a DAST scan told us it was signature-based: it flagged configuration and header problems and a few known CVEs, and missed an issue he already knew was there. What he wanted was a tool that actively probes, tries to bypass controls and shows a real path in. That is the gap between assessment and testing, covered in more depth in[AI pentesting vs traditional DAST](https://codeant.ai/blogs/ai-pentesting-vs-traditional-dast) .


Teams that already run ZAP or Burp still buy outside tests. An engineering leader at a fast-growing software company said his team runs its own exercises with AI and with ZAP or Burp, and still has an outside firm pentest two to three times a year, because[SOC 2](https://www.codeant.ai/blogs/soc-2-penetration-testing-requirements) and customer agreements require it. The reason is simple: you cannot certify your own test. Someone outside has to do it.


Volume is not the same as risk. A security leader at a large enterprise described vulnerability management as wading through hundreds of thousands of findings to find the few that combine into a real problem, and said he wanted tools that come at it from the top down: start from what an attacker can reach and work back to the bugs that matter.


A practical split for a development team:


-


**On every pull request and build:** code review, SAST, dependency and secret scanning, and a DAST scan such as ZAP or StackHawk.


-


**At least once a year, after major releases, and whenever a customer or auditor asks:** a penetration test that proves exploits, covers logged-in roles, and ends with a report.


-


**After every fix:** a retest of the same attack, so you know the fix held.


## What Do Developers Ask Before Adding a VAPT Tool?


-


**Who has to run it?** Every tool in the table needs someone to own it. Burp and ZAP need your engineers' time. A pentest service needs a few hours of scoping and, for grey box, test accounts. One engineering lead listed the hidden cost of a traditional pentest: provisioning accounts, briefing testers, documenting everything, fixing, then removing their access.


-


**Will it flood us with false positives?** Scanners report possibilities, so expect triage. Tools that prove each finding with an exploit, or that check whether a vulnerable path is reachable, cut the noise. Ask any vendor what share of its findings come with proof.


-


**Can it break production?** Ask for the vendor's rules of engagement in writing: which environments, which hours, and how to stop a test at once. Scanners can be noisy too, so the same question applies to DAST in staging and production.


-


**Do we pay per developer, per test or per finding?** Scanners and developer tools usually charge per user (StackHawk) or per plan (Astra). Pentests usually charge per test (Intruder, Aikido) or per scope. Compare a full year: scanner seats plus the number of pentests your customers and auditors expect.

## How Do You Choose the Right VAPT Tool for Your Team?


-


**You need build-time feedback and have no budget:** start with OWASP ZAP in CI.


-


**Your developers write much of their code with AI agents:** look at StackHawk Wingman for checks before a pull request merges.


-


**You have an AppSec engineer who tests by hand:** Burp Suite Professional.


-


**You want a scanner and a pentest from one vendor with list prices:** Astra.


-


**You need a same-day web app pentest with an auditor refund:** Intruder.


-


**You already use Aikido for code scanning:** its pentest module keeps everything in one tool.


-


**You owe an auditor, bank partner or enterprise customer a pentest, need every finding proven, and want black, grey and white box under one offer with a report in 48 hours:** CodeAnt AI.


Most teams end up with two: a scanner in the pipeline and a pentest that proves what the scanner can only suspect.
